rationale: A wins because it gives the founder four clean, pitchable story shapes and mostly keeps its hands on the facts. Its "Educators call gamified learning shallow. Duolingo's answer is a talking cartoon." has real tension without pretending engagement equals learning; B opens with "Duolingo says people are talking to its cartoon owl" even though the update says Lily, not the owl. B asks sharp proof questions, but getting the central character wrong in the headline is the kind of mistake that gets a pitch deleted before the clever strategy paragraph has a chance to breathe.
gaps_in_A: "priciest tier" is not in the update. The facts say paid Max subscribers get the feature; tier hierarchy and pricing need confirmation before the markets angle uses that phrase.
"it's a top-of-funnel move, not an upsell" overstates the chess inference. Free-for-all-users supports the possibility, but the company motive is not supplied.

"live spoken conversation practice is exactly what critics say apps lack" decorates the educator critique. The update only says some educators criticized gamification as shallow learning; it does not give their specific complaint.
gaps_in_B: "cartoon owl" is wrong for the supplied feature. The update says users video-call Lily; confusing Lily with Duolingo's owl is a core fact miss.
"being published for the first time" is invented. The update gives a beta engagement number; it does not say when or whether that number was first disclosed.
"most-criticized design" inflates "some educators have publicly criticized gamification" into a ranking the facts do not support.
"No current news signal anchoring it" ignores the actual launch. Sending the founder to `newsjack-detector` first is make-work when the company update already provides the why-now.
